summary: Gives requirements for adding optical switching support to GSMPv3. It also has clarifications and suggested changes to the GSMPv3 specification. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A controller tells a switch how to connect lines. This memo lists what is needed so it can control light-based switches.

subtitle: Requirements for controlling optical switches and cross-connects

tldr.problem: The GSMP protocol was designed to let controllers manage ATM and Frame Relay switches. As optical switching becomes important, controllers need to manage optical cross-connects and photonic networks using the same protocol.
tldr.mechanism: GSMP needs new label types for optical signals, extended configuration messages to describe optical ports, and transaction models suited to optical switching performance characteristics.
tldr.outcome: Controllers can direct optical switches using GSMP, enabling IP-based optical routers and dynamic optical networks, though implementers also need clarifications on message formats and transaction handling.

facts.label: Supported optical label types
facts.value: DS-1, E1, OC-3, STM-1, VT1.5, VC-12, PDH, G.709 OTN, lambdas, fibers

today: RFC 3604 is Informational and describes requirements rather than a protocol specification. These requirements informed the design of related protocols like GMPLS for controlling optical networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
GSMP (General Switch Management Protocol) lets a controller direct a switch to connect inputs to outputs. The controller can create branches (connections) and give the switch detailed instructions about what to do with traffic.

GSMPv3 works well for ATM and Frame Relay switches, but optical networks introduce new challenges. Optical switches must handle different signal types: wavelengths (lambdas), SONET/SDH hierarchies (like OC-3, STS-1), and TDM signals. These are longer, richer labels than ATM or Frame Relay ports. A single fiber can carry multiple wavelengths, and a single wavelength can carry multiple lower-speed signals.

This memo lists what GSMP needs to support optical switches, and also notes clarifications that implementers of even the current version need.
sections.plainLanguage: A network director tells switches where to send data. This guide says how the director must talk differently to switches made for light signals instead of telephone wires.

sections.title: New Requirements for Optical Switches
sections.content:
Labels must expand to describe optical entities. The memo proposes alignment with GMPLS (Generalized MPLS) to support Digital Carrier labels (DS-1, E1), SONET/SDH labels (OC-3, STM-1, VT1.5, VC-12), PDH labels, OTN G.709 labels, individual wavelengths, and entire fibers. GSMP MUST also handle label hierarchies and lists—for example, five OC-3s grouped together or a contiguous set of wavelengths.

Configuration needs major extensions. Optical switches may support switching at multiple layers simultaneously, so they must report which layers (STS-3c, STS-1, VT-1.5, DS3, DS1) they can handle. Port configuration messages need to report which wavelengths and signals are available, what transport layers are supported on each port, and which lower-layer signals can be multiplexed into higher ones. Ports also need to identify tens of thousands of connections across hundreds of shelves, requiring a Bay/Shelf/Slot/Port locator instead of just Slot/Port.

Service models must define parameters for optical technologies. For transparent optical paths, the controller needs to manage re-timing and re-shaping. For SONET/SDH, the controller must set adaptation parameters when one signal is mapped into another.
sections.plainLanguage: Optical switches carry different kinds of signals stacked inside each other, like envelopes inside envelopes. The director needs to understand all the layers, which signals fit in which envelopes, and where everything is plugged in.

sections.title: Protection and Transactions
sections.content:
Optical networks need fast protection switching. If a link fails, a backup link takes over within about 50 milliseconds. To achieve this, optical cross-connects use hardware-based protection schemes (like ring protection) without waiting for the controller to approve the switch. This means GSMP must let the controller pre-provision the switch's autonomous protection behavior: what to do if a link fails, which backup links to choose, and when to revert to the original link.

The memo describes two protection patterns. 1:n shared protection lets a backup link protect any of several working links. 1+1 dedicated protection sends traffic on both a working path and a protection path; the egress switch automatically chooses the working path if it is healthy, or the protection path if the working path fails.

Optical switches also differ in transaction handling. Many older switches use a serial transaction model—they can handle only one command at a time. Distributed control needs a parallel model, where multiple commands can be in flight. The protocol needs a way to tell the controller whether the switch requires serial or parallel. Additionally, sending multiple transactions in a single message is a useful optimization for slow TDM setups.
sections.plainLanguage: If a light path breaks, a backup light path takes over instantly. The director tells the switch ahead of time which backup path to use and when to give up waiting and switch back. The director also needs to know if the switch can handle multiple orders at the same time or one at a time.

sections.title: Optical Burst Switching
sections.content:
Optical burst switching reserves time on the network for data. Instead of setting up a permanent connection, a burst switch sets up a connection for a specific start time and duration. A connection can be a one-time reservation or repeated.

When a controller requests a burst connection, it gives the switch a start time and duration. The switch performs admission control for that time window and, if the connection is allowed, reserves that exact bandwidth. The switch then autonomously performs the switching at the scheduled time using synchronization methods appropriate for the burst network.
sections.plainLanguage: A burst switch is like reserving a time slot on a railroad: you tell it what time you want to send light, how long, and it makes sure the path is clear then.

sections.title: Clarifications for Implementers
sections.content:
The memo also addresses ambiguities in GSMPv3 itself. When a message is too large for the link, it must be split across multiple segments. The spec added an "I" flag and submessage number, but did not clarify whether the submessage number starts at 0 or 1, or what the I flag means in unsegmented messages.

The Transaction Identifier should distinguish between replies to "AckAll" requests and "NoSuccessAck" requests, and should identify which controller is replying when multiple controllers are connected to one switch. Events should not be allowed to set the "ReturnReceipt" flag.

The Window Size for flow control needs clarification: does it apply to all messages, or only to those that will always generate a reply? If a message may not generate a reply, when should it be removed from the window? Should the window reset if the connection drops and recovers?
sections.plainLanguage: When messages are split into pieces, the spec was vague about which piece is first and what each piece's label means. Implementers also need clearer rules about when to expect replies and how to manage backpressure.
